articles.metaDescription: An honest comparison of salon booking software in 2026: BookReady, Fresha, Vagaro, GlossGenius, Square, and Booksy. Real fees, real tradeoffs, no fluff.
articles.italicTagline: Six platforms, real fee math, and who each one is actually for.
articles.intro: 200-240 word intro. The honest angle: most salon-software comparisons are written by the platforms themselves (note that Zenoti, Booksy, and Square all rank for this term with their own roundups) or by directories paid per lead. Promise an independent read: the criteria that actually matter for a beauty business (storefront design, fee structure, deposits, multi-staff, migration), then six platforms scored against them, then a clear who-should-pick-what. Name the real tension early: feature count is easy to compare, but the public booking page your clients see is what sells, and that is where most platforms are weak. No em-dashes, no superlatives, confident.

sections.title: The 60-second answer
sections.directives: Bulleted verdict (6 bullets): best for design-led owners (BookReady), best free tier (Fresha, with fee caveat), best for retail/POS (Vagaro), best solo POS (GlossGenius), best Square-loyal (Square Appointments), best marketplace (Booksy). Then 80 words framing. Link /pricing/. 150-180 words.

sections.title: The five criteria that actually matter for a salon
sections.directives: Explain the scoring lens, not generic feature lists: (1) the public storefront and template quality, (2) true cost including transaction markup and per-staff fees, (3) deposits and no-show protection, (4) multi-staff and booth-renter handling, (5) how hard it is to leave (data ownership, migration). Argue feature-count is a trap. Link /platform/website/templates/ and /platform/tools/payments/. 200-240 words.

sections.title: The six platforms, scored
sections.directives: Comparison table (.br-compare): rows = the five criteria + monthly price + transaction markup; columns = BookReady, Fresha, Vagaro, GlossGenius, Square, Booksy. Then 120 words honest commentary on the spread. Be fair: cite Fresha's strength (free, marketplace) and weakness (new-client fee). Link /compare/fresha-alternative/ and /compare/vagaro-alternative/. 280-320 words.

sections.title: What each one actually costs once fees are counted
sections.directives: Fee math for a two-chair salon at $10K/mo: subscription + per-staff add-ons + transaction markup, annualized. Show BookReady Studio $49/mo + 0% markup vs the stacked-fee competitors. Be specific with real fee structures (per-staff fees on Booksy, new-client fees on Fresha). Link /pricing/. 220-260 words.

sections.title: The part most comparisons skip: the page your clients see
sections.directives: Make the storefront case. Most platforms ship a functional but generic booking widget. Contrast BookReady's seven editorial templates (The Fade Room, Lush Studio, Velvet Theory, Blackline, Opaline, Petale, Bottega). A beauty business sells aesthetic, and the site is the aesthetic. Link /templates/. 200-240 words.

sections.title: A three-question decision framework
sections.directives: Three questions: (1) do you sell a look (design-led: BookReady, GlossGenius)? (2) do you need marketplace traffic right now (Fresha, Booksy)? (3) do you run heavy retail or in-person POS (Vagaro, Square)? State the BookReady opinion plainly: salons open 12+ months should own their site. Link /pricing/. 180-220 words.

sections.title: When BookReady is the wrong pick
sections.directives: Trust-builder. Choose elsewhere if: you need barcode retail inventory and POS hardware (Vagaro), you depend on marketplace discovery to fill a brand-new chair (Fresha, Booksy), or you run group-class memberships as core revenue. Honest. 150-180 words.

faqs.q: What is the best salon booking software in 2026?
faqs.answerHint: It depends on whether you sell design, need a marketplace, or run heavy retail. BookReady wins on storefront design and 0% fees, Vagaro on retail, Fresha on free marketplace. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a salon booking app and salon booking software?
faqs.answerHint: Mostly marketing. An app emphasizes the phone experience, software the back office. What matters is the booking page clients see and the fees you pay. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: Which salon software has the lowest transaction fees?
faqs.answerHint: BookReady charges 0% on top of Stripe's standard rate (about 2.9% + 30 cents). Most others stack a markup or per-booking fee. 30-50 words.

faqs.q: Is free salon booking software actually free?
faqs.answerHint: Rarely. Free tiers usually recover cost through new-client fees, processing markup, or marketplace commissions. Read the fee page, not the headline. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: Can I move my client list between platforms?
faqs.answerHint: Most platforms export a client CSV. BookReady runs the import for free during migration, usually same-day. 30-50 words.

faqs.q: Which is best for a multi-stylist salon?
faqs.answerHint: BookReady Salon ($99/mo) for a designed multi-staff site, or Vagaro if you have serious retail. Both handle staff calendars and payouts. 30-50 words.

articles.metaTitle: Can a Salon Charge for a Missed Appointment? | BookReady
articles.metaDescription: Yes, salons can charge for missed appointments, within limits. The rules, fair amounts, and how to set a no-show policy that actually holds up. From BookReady.
articles.h1: Can a salon charge for a missed appointment?
articles.italicTagline: Short answer: yes, with conditions. Here is how to do it right.
articles.primaryKeyword: can a hair salon charge you for a missed appointment
secondaryKeywords: can salons charge for no shows
articles.intro: 180-220 word intro. Answer the question in the first two sentences (yes, salons can charge for missed appointments, as long as the policy was disclosed and the fee is reasonable). Then frame why it gets confusing: the fee has to be communicated up front and cannot exceed the service value. This piece is written for owners deciding how to set a defensible policy, but it answers the client-side question honestly too, which is what builds trust and rankings. Preview: the rules, fair amounts, card-on-file vs deposit, making it enforceable, the human script. No em-dashes, plain, authoritative.

sections.title: Yes, but only under two conditions
sections.directives: State the two conditions plainly: (1) the policy was disclosed before booking, (2) the fee is reasonable relative to the service (cannot charge $300 for a $200 service). Note that the vast majority of stylists do charge no-show fees. Set expectation that 'reasonable + disclosed' is the whole game. 150-180 words.

sections.title: What the law actually allows
sections.directives: Explain without pretending to be legal advice: businesses can charge cancellation and no-show fees, but they are limited to a reasonable amount and require prior disclosure. Typical fair range: 30-50% for late cancellation with notice, up to 100% for a true no-show with no notice. Recommend the reader confirm local rules. Be careful and honest. 200-240 words.

sections.title: How much to charge so it holds and does not feel hostile
sections.directives: Give concrete guidance by scenario: late cancel inside the window (forfeit deposit or 50%), full no-show (100% of service or the card on file), chronic offender (move to deposit-required). Tie to deposit best practices. Link /guides/deposit-best-practices/ and /guides/no-show-fee-policy/. 200-240 words.

sections.title: Card on file vs deposit: how the charge actually happens
sections.directives: Explain the two mechanisms: an upfront deposit at booking, or a card-on-file charged after a no-show. Tradeoffs (deposit = stronger protection, card-on-file = lower booking friction). Walk through how BookReady handles both through Stripe. Link /platform/tools/payments/. 180-220 words.

sections.title: The policy only holds if it is visible in three places
sections.directives: The enforceability rule: the policy must appear at booking (before confirm), in the confirmation, and in the reminder. If it is not in all three, a disputed charge is hard to win. Link /guides/cancellation-policy-template/ and /platform/tools/notifications/. 180-220 words.

sections.title: What to say when you charge the fee
sections.directives: Provide short SMS scripts for: first-time offender (warm, offer rebook), repeat offender (move to deposit-required), genuine emergency (waive gracefully). Kind, firm, brief. 200-240 words.

faqs.q: Can a salon legally charge me for a no-show?
faqs.answerHint: Yes, if the policy was disclosed before you booked and the fee is reasonable. It generally cannot exceed the price of the service. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: How much can a salon charge for a missed appointment?
faqs.answerHint: Commonly 30-50% for a late cancellation with notice, up to 100% of the service for a true no-show. The fee must be reasonable and disclosed. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: Can a salon charge my card without telling me?
faqs.answerHint: Not fairly. The policy must be visible before you book. A charge tied to a clearly disclosed policy is enforceable, a surprise charge usually is not. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: What if I had a real emergency?
faqs.answerHint: Most salons waive the fee for genuine emergencies. Reach out, explain, and offer to rebook. Good owners value the relationship over one fee. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: How do salons enforce no-show fees?
faqs.answerHint: Usually with a deposit at booking or a card on file charged after the no-show, both through a processor like Stripe. 30-50 words.

sections.title: Why reminders are your cheapest no-show insurance
sections.directives: Make the case with specifics: a 2-touch sequence cuts no-shows roughly 20%, a 3-touch with a reply request 40-60%. Frame reminders as respect for both calendars, not nagging. Link /guides/reducing-no-shows/. 160-200 words.

sections.directives: Specify the cadence: (1) confirmation immediately on booking, (2) reminder 48 hours out with a reply request, (3) day-of text 4 hours before with address and parking. Explain the why of each touch. Link /platform/tools/notifications/. 180-220 words.

sections.title: Copy-paste SMS reminder templates
sections.directives: Provide 5-6 real SMS templates in styled callouts with [BRACKETED] merge fields: booking confirmation, 48-hour reply-required, day-of, running-late-from-salon, and a warm win-back for a missed slot. Keep each short and on-brand. 240-280 words including templates.

sections.title: The wording rules that make clients reply

faqs.q: When should I send appointment reminders?
faqs.answerHint: A confirmation at booking, a reminder 48 hours out, and a day-of text about 4 hours before. That 3-touch cadence cuts no-shows most. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: Should appointment reminders be text or email?
faqs.answerHint: Both. Text gets opened fast and is best for the 48-hour and day-of nudges; email is better for confirmations and prep notes. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: What should a salon reminder text say?
faqs.answerHint: Name the client and stylist, the date and time, and make it one tap to confirm or reschedule. Keep it short and on-brand. 40-60 words.

faqs.q: Do reminder messages actually reduce no-shows?
faqs.answerHint: Yes. A 2-touch sequence cuts no-shows around 20%, a 3-touch with a reply request 40-60%. 30-50 words.

faqs.q: Can I personalize reminders for each client?
faqs.answerHint: Yes. Merge fields fill in the name, stylist, service, and time automatically, so every message reads personal without manual work. 40-60 words.
